title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
summary: Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.
content: Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." The red nova designated AT 2025abao and its location in the Andromeda galaxy (Image credit: Palomar Observatory/ZTF/WINTER, Viraj Karambelkar) An important clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star. When Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025. The four main stages in the evolution of AT2025abao. The red giant swells out, enveloping its smaller companion star, which is then dragged into its core, ejecting material that caused a flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025. (Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI)) One of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Big Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier. This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass. "It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Big and Little Bao," Karambelkar said. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries." The team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

title: Artemis III astronauts meet their spacecraft | Space photo of the day for Nov. 27, 2026
content: NASA's Artemis III astronauts pose holding up three fingers to symbolize their mission as they visit the Orion spacecraft they will ride to space. (Image credit: NASA/Kim Shiflett) Training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates. What is it? Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding. In the snapshot , the crew — from left to right, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick (mission commander) and Frank Rubio (mission specialist), European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano (mission pilot) and NASA astronaut Andre Douglas (mission specialist) — is spotted posing alongside the same Orion spacecraft that they will fly to space as part of their mission. This brief moment of levity took place where the spacecraft currently resides at the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Why is it incredible? This crew has a serious mission ahead of them. The four astronauts will launch to low-Earth orbit around Earth where they plan to practice rendezvous and docking with both Blue Origin and SpaceX's lunar landing vehicles , Blue Moon and Starship, respectively. To prepare, the crew has to undergo months of critical training to both be physically ready while prepared to handle any situation that might come up during their mission. And while Artemis III isn't landing astronauts on the moon, it is a critical step toward that goal. If Artemis III goes to plan and NASA has a lunar landing vehicle that passes rendezvous and docking tests with the Orion spacecraft, Artemis IV might see astronauts land on the moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
summary: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. Here's why it mattered.
content: On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting. (Image credit: Alto Vintage Images/Alamy) Why it mattered Not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible. But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name). Meteor Shower Quiz: How Well Do You Know 'Shooting Stars'? This modern photo of the Geminid meteor shower shows dozens of meteors captured in a long exposure by Josh Drury. Ladislaus Weinek, who captured the first photo of a meteor, had to use a photographic plate in 1889. (Image credit: Josh Dury) Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days. Instead of photographic plates or digital cameras, astronomers now have to use special tracking equipment to record images of Andromedid meteors. In 2011, astronomers announced that the meteor shower seemed to be undergoing a resurgence of activity, with 50 meteors per hour, and upticks were expected in 2018 and 2023. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

Here's how to check if a website is secure. Look at the address bar at the top of the browser. Make sure the address matches the website you think you're on. Look for a padlock icon by the address bar. Not all browsers offer this but if you see it it's a sign your details will be secure. If there's no padlock icon, your browser will have another icon, such as Firefox's shield, or Google Chrome's tune icon. Look for the words 'connection secure'. Even if the website isn't an imitation, it's important to be wary of sites that pop up offering massive discounts. If you see one of the best smart telescopes for a quarter of its normal price, for example, you should immediately be suspicious. Your credit card or debit card may offer some protection if you are scammed but you should always be wary. Other warnings include misspelled product names, stock text, buttons that don't work and other oddities. You can also use a domain name checker to find out how old a website is. title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
summary: The queen in the northern night sky is supposedly one of the easiest constellations to recognize — you just look for a W. Or is that an M?
content: Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Big Dipper /the Plough. It's gone. Nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn. What's happening and when to look Stars move anti-clockwise around the north celestial pole, so Cassiopeia changes orientation. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) Late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you look, it can look like a W, E, M or a 3. This is because Cassiopeia is circumpolar. Rather than rising in the east and eventually setting in the west like many familiar constellations , it circles the north celestial pole — a position currently held by Polaris , the North Star. From sufficiently northerly latitudes, its main stars never disappear below the horizon. This gives us a simple observing experiment. Find Cassiopeia in the early evening and remember its orientation relative to the horizon. Go back several hours later and look again. The constellation has moved around Polaris, and its shape has changed. The stars haven't changed their arrangement — Earth has simply rotated from west to east. We all know this logically, but watching the familiar pattern of Cassiopeia's stars apparently tip over during a single night makes Earth's rotation a lot less abstract. How and when I'm watching it The names and distances of the stars in Cassiopeia. (Image credit: Starry Night) I'm going to observe Cassiopeia twice on the same evening this week, which is about as complicated as the experiment needs to get. The first time will be shortly after darkness falls. I'll find the W, note which way it seems to be pointing and use something fixed — a rooftop, tree or chimney — to give myself a rough reference for its position. I'll return to my backyard before bed, and see where the pattern has shifted. Cassiopeia's main stars are bright enough to survive urban and suburban light pollution, so you don't need a particularly dark sky or a telescope. While I'm gazing at Cassiopeia, I'll try to see the stars as they really are, and not just how they appear to us. Check out the distances of its stars from the sun : Caph: 55 light-years Schedar: 228 light-years Navi: 550 light-years Ruchbah: 99 light-years Segin: 440 light-years Only Caph and Ruchbah are within 100 light-years — the sun's local interstellar neighborhood. Does that destroy the very concept of Cassiopeia as a group of related stars? Cassiopeia, like all constellations, is a mirage, with a capital M. There's another reason I love Cassiopeia. Proxima Centauri, the closest star to our sun, lies just 4.24 light-years away. Travel there and look back towards our solar system , and our sun would appear as an extra star in Cassiopeia — effectively giving the constellation a sixth bright point. From a certain perspective, we are all Cassiopeians. Stargazer's corner: Nov. 27-Dec. 4, 2026 NGC 457 (the Owl Cluster) is in Cassiopeia. (Image credit: Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) The last few evenings of November bring back darker early-night skies as the moon wanes from full earlier in the week and rises progressively later. It will rise in the middle of the night as it reaches its last-quarter phase on Dec. 1. It's an ideal time to sweep a pair of binoculars across the rich star fields around Cassiopeia and Perseus . On the boundary between the two constellations is the Double Cluster (NGC 869 and NGC 884), one of the finest binocular sights in the entire northern sky. These two dense concentrations of young stars sit side by side against the richer background of the Milky Way . Under a dark sky, you can see it with the naked eye. M52, NGC 457 (the Owl Cluster) and NGC 663 are other clusters also worth seeking out in Cassiopeia. Conjunction of the week: Moon, Jupiter, Mars and Regulus Four objects will trace a striking crescent on Nov. 30. (Image credit: Starry Night) Get outside about 45 minutes before sunrise on Monday, Nov. 30, and look high in the southern sky for a fitting month-ending finale. A 61%-lit waning gibbous moon will appear alongside brilliant Jupiter , reddish Mars and Regulus, the brightest star in Leo. Together, the four objects will trace a striking crescent spanning just over five degrees of sky — roughly the width of three fingers held at arm's length. It's a much tighter version of a similar arrangement visible on Nov. 2, with Jupiter by far the brightest point and the contrasting colors of Mars and blue-white Regulus adding to the spectacle. No equipment will be needed, though binoculars will help you get a close-up of this rather unusual conjunction.

title: Dropping missiles from orbit? 2 European companies sign agreement to study the idea
summary: Atmos Space Cargo will fly its first Phoenix cargo-return capsule on SpaceX's Bandwagon 3 rideshare mission, which is scheduled to launch this spring.
content: A pair of companies in Europe have signed an agreement to study the feasibility of developing weapons that can be dropped from orbit. Atmos, a space company known for its Phoenix reusable reentry vehicle , will work with MBDA, Europe's largest missile manufacturer, on the new project. "We are assessing how proven defense systems and new orbital technologies can be combined to strengthen Europe's conventional deterrence and enable future defense capabilities," Sebastian Klaus, the CEO of Atmos Space Cargo, said in a statement on Nov. 18. The system that the companies are investigating is called Precision Orbital Deep Strike, or PODS. The companies said that their initial scope will center on design and feasibility, as well as technology integration. Atmos and MBDA also said this work could lead to demonstrations, but the companies' announcement makes it clear that any deployment or use would be subject to the approval of governmental and military authorities. "The initiative also directly supports MBDA's broader strategic vision in the space domain, reinforcing both space for defense and the defense of space," Thomas Gottschild, MBDA Deutschland managing director, said in the same statement. This news comes a few months after Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said that the U.S. Space Force operates orbital weapons . "Let me be crystal clear: Today, Guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks," Schiess said during a conferenace presentation on Sept. 15 ("Guardians" refers to Space Force personnel.) Last year, Atmos' Phoenix capsule got its first test run in space. The cargo-return technology launched aboard a Space X Falcon 9 rocket during a rideshare mission in February 2025. Atmos tested out the inflatable heat shields it has been working on to help future space-manufactured cargo make it through Earth's atmosphere in one piece. "Orbital transportation and return form a new layer of strategic infrastructure, and infrastructure determines what Europe can achieve on its own terms," Klaus said in the Nov 18 statement.
